target_customer: Software developers and engineering organizations that build, ship and run containerized applications; enterprises pay for subscriptions
problem: Developers hit works on my machine problems moving code between environments, and operators wanted isolated, dense, portable workloads.
business_model: Open source core with paid developer subscriptions (Docker Desktop, Hub) and formerly an enterprise platform

founders.name: Solomon Hykes
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder on the YC page. Education and prior employers not found in opened sources.

founders.name: Kamel Founadi
founders.background_notes: Named by Wikipedia as a founder of dotCloud; not on the YC page.

founders.name: Sebastien Pahl
founders.background_notes: Named by Wikipedia as a founder of dotCloud; not on the YC page.

competitors.name: Heroku
competitors.what: Platform as a service for Ruby, Rack and Node.js apps
competitors.traction_then: Named by trade press as a leading PaaS host

competitors.name: Engine Yard
competitors.what: Platform as a service host focused on Ruby on Rails
competitors.traction_then: Named by trade press as a PaaS example

technical_complexity.rationale: Multi-language cloud platform built on Linux isolation primitives was hard for a small team; later container runtime and image tooling required deep systems engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Open source container format and Hub registry built a large developer ecosystem, but Kubernetes and OCI standards later commoditized the runtime.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Red Hat partnered with Docker in 2013; the dotCloud brand and tech were sold to cloudControl in August 2014; Docker Enterprise was sold to Mirantis in November 2019.

market_need_then: Developers in 2010 were adopting PaaS hosts such as Heroku and Engine Yard to avoid managing servers, showing demand for simpler deployment; dotCloud aimed at a multi-language version of that.

branding.name_origin: Company renamed from dotCloud to Docker, Inc. on October 29, 2013 after the container project; the source does not explain why the name was chosen.
branding.domain_note: Uses docker.com; acquisition history not found.

identity.logo: A blue whale carrying shipping containers
identity.mascot_or_character: Moby Dock, a whale; community vote on the name dated September 2013 by a forum post

branding.brand_signature: The Moby Dock whale carrying containers

rebrands.why: Company refocused on the Docker container project

branding.community_and_virality: Docker sponsored a real whale named Molly Dock in June 2015 per Network World; community voted on the mascot name per a Docker forum post. Some details rest on low quality blogs.

brand_strength.rationale: The whale mascot and the Docker name became synonymous with containers among developers; the rename to Docker came with the project's rapid adoption.

pivots.from: dotCloud, a multi-language platform as a service
pivots.why: The open source Docker container engine drew far more adoption than the PaaS

pivots.to: Developer tools focus (Desktop and Hub) after selling Docker Enterprise to Mirantis
pivots.why: Restructuring and recapitalization with a $35M investment

outcome_analysis: Docker began as the PaaS dotCloud and found its real market by open sourcing its container engine in 2013, raising large rounds up to a reported 1 billion dollar valuation in 2015. Kubernetes and monetization problems led to the 2019 sale of Docker Enterprise to Mirantis and a recapitalization, after which a developer tools focus led to a reported 2.1 billion dollar valuation in 2022. It remains active and independent.
notes: Funding figures rest on Wikipedia, cross-checked by Fortune (2015 Series D, snippet), SDxCentral (2019) and aggregator snippets; totals differ across databases ($197M to $434M). A 2017 Series E of about $92M appears only on one database and is not recorded as a round. The Series C 2014 valuation of $400M is attributed to Fortune via a search snippet. Round labels for 2019 onward restart at Series A in sources; recorded as other. The Mirantis sale was a partial asset sale, not an exit of the company. Layoff claims in forums are unverified. Heroku and Engine Yard sources are dated Nov 2010, a few months after the Summer 2010 batch.
